blocks.x: Chapter 7 is about pictures of equations, and drawing one takes a way to name a single point by numbers. Two number lines set at right angles are enough. One runs left and right, the other up and down, so every point has two counts, how far along and how far up. The first problem reads those counts off a walk, the second turns on their order.

The pair naming a point lists the count along first and the count up second, so a place 6 units along and 4 units up from where the two number lines cross is written \((6,4)\). A beetle starts at that crossing point, walks 11 units along, turns around and walks 3 units back the way it came, then walks 5 units up. Enter the first number of the pair naming where the beetle stops.
hints: The first number of the pair is how far along the beetle ends up, not how far it walked in total. Work that count out from the moves along and leave the 5 units up out of it.
Walking 3 units back the way it came undoes part of the 11 units out, so the ending count along is smaller than 11.
blocks.sol: The beetle ends up \(11-3=8\) units along and \(5\) units up, so its pair is \((8,5)\) and the first number is \(\boxed{8}\). Adding the two moves along instead of subtracting gives \(14\), which is the total distance walked along and not the place the beetle stops.

blocks.x: Three points are \((6,21)\), \((21,6)\) and \((13,27)\). One of them sits furthest to the right. Enter the second number of that point's pair.
hints: How far right a point sits comes from the first number of its pair, not the second. Compare the three first numbers before anything else.
The first numbers are \(6\), \(21\) and \(13\), so one point is clearly furthest right. Read off that point's second number.
blocks.sol: The first number of a pair is how far along, and those are \(6\), \(21\) and \(13\), so \((21,6)\) sits furthest to the right and its second number is \(\boxed{6}\). Swapping the two roles would make \((13,27)\) look furthest right and give \(27\), which is why the order inside a pair is fixed.

blocks.x: An ordered pair names a point. Two number lines at right angles form the coordinate plane. The horizontal one is the \(x\)-axis, the vertical one is the \(y\)-axis, and they cross at the origin, \((0,0)\). The pair \((a,b)\) names the point reached by going \(a\) along the \(x\)-axis and \(b\) up the \(y\)-axis, so \(a\) is its \(x\)-coordinate and \(b\) its \(y\)-coordinate. Negative \(a\) means left and negative \(b\) means down. The pair is ordered, \(x\) first and \(y\) second, so \((3,7)\) and \((7,3)\) are different points.

A point sits \(6\) units to the left of the \(y\)-axis and \(3\) units below the \(x\)-axis. A second point sits \(10\) units further left, at the same height. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the second point.
hints: Fix both coordinates of the first point before moving anything, and remember that left of the \(y\)-axis puts its \(x\)-coordinate below zero.
Moving further left subtracts, so the second \(x\)-coordinate is \(10\) less than the first. The height is the same for both points and is not needed here.
blocks.sol: The first point is \(6\) to the left, so \(x=-6\), and \(3\) below, so \(y=-3\). Moving \(10\) further left subtracts \(10\), giving \(-6-10=\boxed{-16}\). Further left always means a smaller \(x\)-coordinate. Adding the \(10\) instead gives \(4\), which sits on the other side of the \(y\)-axis entirely.

blocks.x: One of the points \((0,-19)\) and \((-19,0)\) lies on the \(x\)-axis, and the other lies on the \(y\)-axis. Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the one that lies on the \(y\)-axis.
hints: The origin \((0,0)\) lies on the \(y\)-axis, and so does every point directly above or below it. Work out what those points all share in their first coordinate.

Both pairs contain a \(0\), so the position of that \(0\) is what decides. A first coordinate of \(0\) means \(x=0\), which is the \(y\)-axis, and a second coordinate of \(0\) means \(y=0\), which is the \(x\)-axis.
blocks.sol: Every point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x\)-coordinate \(0\), so \((0,-19)\) is the one on the \(y\)-axis, and its \(y\)-coordinate is \(\boxed{-19}\). The common mistake is the reversal, since a coordinate of \(0\) puts a point on the axis named by the other letter. So \(x=0\) gives the \(y\)-axis, \(y=0\) gives the \(x\)-axis, and picking \((-19,0)\) would have given \(0\).

blocks.x: A point is on an axis exactly when one of its coordinates is zero. A point with \(x=0\) is no distance along from the origin, so it sits on the vertical axis, the \(y\)-axis. A point with \(y=0\) is at no height, so it sits on the horizontal axis, the \(x\)-axis. The coordinate set to zero is never the one the axis is named after. The origin has both coordinates zero and lies on both axes. The two axes cut the rest of the plane into four regions, each one a quadrant, and a point of either axis is on a boundary rather than inside a region, so it is in no quadrant.

blocks.cap: The \(x\)-axis and the \(y\)-axis cross at the origin and cut the plane into four quadrants, numbered counterclockwise from the upper right. The gold point walks \(3\) along and then \(2\) up, which is exactly what the pair \((3,2)\) says to do. Neither axis belongs to a quadrant, and the lower band shows the two axis cases.

blocks.x: Those four regions are the quadrants, numbered counterclockwise from the upper right, as in the figure. Which side of the \(y\)-axis a point is on depends only on the sign of its \(x\)-coordinate, and which side of the \(x\)-axis only on the sign of its \(y\)-coordinate. The next two problems need nothing beyond those two signs.
A point \((m,n)\) has \(m<0\) and \(n>0\), and nothing else about the two values is known. Enter the number of the quadrant the point lies in.
hints: A negative \(x\)-coordinate means the point is left of the \(y\)-axis, and a positive \(y\)-coordinate means it is above the \(x\)-axis. Name that corner of the plane first.
Left and above is the upper left region. Count counterclockwise from the upper right to reach its number.
blocks.sol: Negative \(x\) means left of the \(y\)-axis and positive \(y\) means above the \(x\)-axis, so the point is in the upper left region, quadrant \(\boxed{2}\). Neither value is needed, only the two signs. Every point with that sign pattern is in the same quadrant, however large or small \(m\) and \(n\) are.

blocks.x: The point \((a,b)\) lies in quadrant two, and nothing else about \(a\) and \(b\) is known. Enter the number of the quadrant that \((b,a)\) lies in.
hints: Get the sign of \(a\) and the sign of \(b\) from quadrant two first, which is left of the \(y\)-axis and above the \(x\)-axis.
So \(a\) is negative and \(b\) is positive. In \((b,a)\) the positive number is the \(x\)-coordinate and the negative one is the \(y\)-coordinate.
blocks.sol: Quadrant two is left of the \(y\)-axis and above the \(x\)-axis, so \(a<0\) and \(b>0\). Then \((b,a)\) has a positive \(x\)-coordinate and a negative \(y\)-coordinate, which is right of the \(y\)-axis and below the \(x\)-axis, quadrant \(\boxed{4}\). The quadrant depends on the signs alone, so no values for \(a\) and \(b\) are needed. In \((a,b)\) the negative number is first and in \((b,a)\) it is second, so the two points lie in different quadrants.

blocks.x: The four quadrants. The axes cut the plane into four regions, numbered counterclockwise from the upper right. Quadrant one contains the points with \(x>0\) and \(y>0\), quadrant two those with \(x<0\) and \(y>0\), quadrant three those with \(x<0\) and \(y<0\), and quadrant four those with \(x>0\) and \(y<0\). Counterclockwise the sign pairs are \((+,+)\), \((-,+)\), \((-,-)\), \((+,-)\), one sign changing at each axis crossed. Nothing depends on the sizes, so \((0.01,900)\) and \((5,5)\) share a quadrant, and a point with a zero coordinate is on an axis and in no quadrant.

Any two points have a distance between them, and when they share a coordinate that distance is already a length on a single number line. Two points at the same height differ only in how far along they sit, so the gap between them is the difference of their \(x\)-coordinates. A distance is never negative, so subtract the smaller from the larger.
The points \((-12,5)\) and \((21,5)\) have the same \(y\)-coordinate, so the segment joining them is horizontal. Enter its length.
hints: Only the \(x\)-values differ, so the length is the distance from \(-12\) to \(21\) on the number line. Counting across \(0\) is a safe way to do it.
The length is \(21-(-12)\). Subtracting a negative adds, so the result is larger than \(21\), not smaller.
blocks.sol: Both endpoints have \(y=5\), so the length is the difference of the \(x\)-coordinates, \(21-(-12)=21+12=\boxed{33}\). Computing \(21-12=9\) instead is what comes of dropping the sign on \(-12\). One endpoint is \(12\) units left of the \(y\)-axis and the other \(21\) units right, so those two distances add.

blocks.x: Pierre de Fermat worked out coordinate geometry on his own, slightly earlier than the version the plane is named for. His manuscript circulated in 1636 but was not printed until after his death, so the idea arrived twice.

The points \(A=(2,-1)\) and \(B=(14,4)\) have no coordinate in common, so a single subtraction will not give the distance. The point \(C=(14,-1)\) lies directly to the right of \(A\) and directly below \(B\), so triangle \(ABC\) has a right angle at \(C\), one leg horizontal and one leg vertical. Find the two leg lengths, then use the Pythagorean theorem. Enter the distance from \(A\) to \(B\).
hints: A horizontal segment has length equal to the difference of the two \(x\)-coordinates, and a vertical segment the difference of the two \(y\)-coordinates. Take each difference in the order that makes it positive, and watch the subtraction of \(-1\).
The legs come out \(12\) and \(5\). The theorem gives the square of \(AB\) as the sum of the squares of those two.
blocks.sol: The horizontal leg is \(14-2=12\) and the vertical leg is \(4-(-1)=5\), so \(AB^2=12^2+5^2=144+25=169\) and \(AB=\sqrt{169}=\boxed{13}\). One leg is horizontal and the other vertical, so the angle between them is right and the theorem applies. Adding the legs gives \(17\), the length of the path through \(C\) rather than the direct distance.

blocks.x: The distance formula. For points \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\), the point \((x_2,y_1)\) is the right-angle corner of a triangle with a horizontal leg of length \(|x_2-x_1|\) and a vertical leg of length \(|y_2-y_1|\), and the angle there is right because the axes meet at right angles. The Pythagorean theorem then gives $$d=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}.$$ Each difference is squared, so its sign has no effect and subtracting in either order gives the same distance. When the two points share a coordinate, one difference is \(0\) and what is left is the single subtraction from before.

The point halfway along the segment joining two points is their midpoint. On a single number line, halfway between two numbers is their average. How far along a point sits and how high it sits are each measured on a number line of their own, so averaging the two coordinates separately is worth a try, and the next two problems check it.
A segment has endpoints \((-6,-5)\) and \((10,19)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the midpoint of that segment.
hints: The midpoint has two coordinates and only one of them is wanted here. The \(-6\) and the \(10\) give the \(x\)-coordinate of the midpoint, and the \(y\)-coordinate comes from the other two numbers.
The \(y\)-coordinate of the midpoint is the average of \(-5\) and \(19\). Add the two heights first, keeping the sign on \(-5\), then halve the total.
blocks.sol: The \(y\)-coordinate of the midpoint is the average of the two endpoint heights, \(\frac{-5+19}{2}=\frac{14}{2}=\boxed{7}\). Counting from the lower end gives the same value, since \(19-(-5)=24\) and half of that added to \(-5\) is \(-5+12=7\).

blocks.x: The midpoint of the segment joining \(A=(-3,9)\) and \(B\) is \(M=(5,-4)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of \(B\).
hints: The midpoint's \(y\)-coordinate is the average of the two endpoints' \(y\)-coordinates. Here that average is known and one of the two numbers being averaged is not.
Call the \(y\)-coordinate of \(B\) simply \(y\) and write \(\frac{9+y}{2}=-4\), then multiply both sides by \(2\) to clear the fraction and solve.
blocks.sol: Write \(B=(x,y)\). The midpoint's \(y\)-coordinate is the average of the two endpoints', so \(\frac{9+y}{2}=-4\), giving \(9+y=-8\) and \(y=\boxed{-17}\). As a check, the drop from \(9\) to \(-4\) is \(13\), and another \(13\) below \(-4\) is \(-17\). Averaging the two given heights gives \(\frac{9+(-4)}{2}=\frac{5}{2}\), the height halfway from \(A\) to \(M\) rather than the height of \(B\).

blocks.x: The midpoint is the average of the coordinates. The midpoint of the segment joining \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\) is $$M=\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right).$$ Going from one endpoint to the other changes the \(x\)-coordinate by \(x_2-x_1\), so half of that change from \(x_1\) is \(x_1+\frac{x_2-x_1}{2}=\frac{x_1+x_2}{2}\), with the same work for the height. Multiplying by \(2\) gives \(x_1+x_2=2x_M\), where \(x_M\) is the midpoint's own \(x\)-coordinate. When one endpoint and the midpoint are known, that leaves the missing coordinate as the only unknown.

Everything in this lesson comes from the two coordinates of a point. Naming a quadrant takes only their signs, a distance between two points takes the two differences, and a midpoint takes the two averages. The last two problems use more than one of the three at once.
A segment runs from \(A=(-7,-2)\) to \(B=(5,14)\), and \(M\) is the midpoint of that segment. Enter the distance from \(A\) to \(M\).
hints: The midpoint is halfway along, so its distance from an endpoint is half the whole length. Finding the whole length first avoids computing the midpoint at all.
The two differences from \(A\) to \(B\) are \(12\) and \(16\). Put those through the distance formula, then halve.
blocks.sol: The differences are \(5-(-7)=12\) and \(14-(-2)=16\), so the whole length is \(\sqrt{12^2+16^2}=\sqrt{400}=20\), and half of it is \(\boxed{10}\). The other route agrees, since the midpoint is \((-1,6)\) and \(\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=\sqrt{100}=10\). Each difference from \(A\) to \(M\) is half the matching difference from \(A\) to \(B\), so halving the whole length gives the same value.

blocks.x: The midpoint of the segment joining \(A=(-3,7)\) and \(B\) lies on the \(x\)-axis, and the \(x\)-coordinate of \(B\) is \(45\). Enter the distance from \(A\) to \(B\).
hints: Only the second coordinate of \(B\) is unknown, so write \(B=(45,k)\). A point of the \(x\)-axis has \(y\)-coordinate \(0\), so the midpoint's second coordinate is known even though the midpoint is not. That is one equation for \(k\).
The two second coordinates average to \(0\), so \(\frac{7+k}{2}=0\). Once \(B\) is known, the two differences are \(48\) and \(-14\).
blocks.sol: Write \(B=(45,k)\). A point of the \(x\)-axis has \(y\)-coordinate \(0\), so \(\frac{7+k}{2}=0\), giving \(k=-7\) and \(B=(45,-7)\). The differences are \(45-(-3)=48\) and \(-7-7=-14\), so the distance is \(\sqrt{48^2+(-14)^2}=\sqrt{2304+196}=\sqrt{2500}=\boxed{50}\). Setting \(x=0\) instead puts the zero on the wrong coordinate, and the \(x\)-coordinate of \(B\) is already given.

blocks.x: The plane is built. Every ordered pair names one point, every point has exactly one pair, and both the distance formula and the midpoint formula come out of that naming alone. Lesson 7.2, Graphing Linear Equations, is about the pairs that make an equation true.

review.x: A point lies \(24\) units to the left of the \(y\)-axis and \(6\) units above the \(x\)-axis. Enter its \(x\)-coordinate.
hints: The \(x\)-coordinate is the horizontal position, measured left or right from the \(y\)-axis, and the \(y\)-coordinate is the vertical position, measured up or down from the \(x\)-axis.
Right of the \(y\)-axis is positive and left of it is negative, so settle the sign first. The \(6\) is a vertical distance, so it belongs to the other coordinate.
review.sol: The horizontal position is the \(x\)-coordinate, and \(24\) units left of the \(y\)-axis is \(24\) units in the negative direction, so the \(x\)-coordinate is \(\boxed{-24}\). The \(6\) units above the \(x\)-axis is the vertical position, so the point is \((-24,6)\).

review.x: The points \((20,-11)\) and \((-11,20)\) are built from the same two numbers in opposite orders. Exactly one of them sits above the \(x\)-axis. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of that point.
hints: A point sits above the \(x\)-axis exactly when its \(y\)-coordinate is positive, and that is the second number of the pair, so compare the two second numbers first.
Both pairs are built from \(20\) and \(-11\), so once you have picked the one above the axis, the trap is entering its second number. The \(x\)-coordinate is the first number.
review.sol: The second numbers are \(-11\) and \(20\), so \((-11,20)\) is the point above the \(x\)-axis, and its \(x\)-coordinate is \(\boxed{-11}\). Answering \(20\) means reading the pair in the wrong order, since \(20\) is that point's \(y\)-coordinate.

review.x: A point lies on the \(y\)-axis, \(26\) units above the origin. Enter its \(x\)-coordinate.
hints: Being on the \(y\)-axis fixes one of the two coordinates. Ask how far you move horizontally from the origin to reach the point, and that horizontal step is the \(x\)-coordinate.
In the pair \((x,y)\), the first number is the horizontal distance from the origin and the second is the vertical distance. The \(26\) units are vertical.
review.sol: A point on the \(y\)-axis sits directly above or below the origin with no horizontal step, so its \(x\)-coordinate is \(\boxed{0}\). The \(26\) is the vertical distance, so the point is \((0,26)\). The common slip is to read \(y\)-axis as \(y=0\), but the coordinate that is \(0\) there is \(x\).

review.x: Seven points are \((-9,2)\), \((0,7)\), \((3,-4)\), \((-1,-1)\), \((8,0)\), \((-5,-6)\) and \((2,9)\). Enter how many of them lie inside a quadrant rather than on an axis.
hints: A point lies on an axis exactly when at least one of its coordinates is zero, so scan the list for zeros before anything else.
Signs do not matter for this count. A pair of negatives such as \((-5,-6)\) has no zero in it, so it still lies inside a quadrant.
review.sol: Of the seven, \((0,7)\) and \((8,0)\) have a zero coordinate and so are on an axis, which leaves \(\boxed{5}\). A point is on an axis whenever either of its coordinates is zero, and no point on an axis is inside a quadrant.

review.x: Enter the number of the quadrant containing the point \((-2.5,-40)\).
hints: A quadrant depends only on the two signs, so the sizes \(2.5\) and \(40\) can be ignored entirely.
Both coordinates are negative, so the point is left of the \(y\)-axis and below the \(x\)-axis. Count counterclockwise from the upper right.
review.sol: The first coordinate is negative, so the point is left of the \(y\)-axis, and the second is negative, so the point is below the \(x\)-axis. That is the lower left region, quadrant \(\boxed{3}\). The sizes \(2.5\) and \(40\) make no difference, since a quadrant depends only on the two signs.

review.x: The product of a point's two coordinates is positive, and its \(x\)-coordinate is positive. Enter the number of the quadrant the point lies in.
hints: A product of two numbers is positive when the two share a sign, and two negatives share a sign just as well as two positives.
The \(x\)-coordinate is stated positive, so the shared sign is positive and the \(y\)-coordinate is positive too.
review.sol: A positive product means the two coordinates share a sign, and the \(x\)-coordinate is positive, so the \(y\)-coordinate is positive as well. Right of the \(y\)-axis and above the \(x\)-axis is quadrant \(\boxed{1}\). Without the fact about \(x\), both coordinates could be negative instead, which is quadrant three.

review.x: The point \((c+5,\ c+12)\) lies on the \(x\)-axis. Enter \(c\).
hints: A point on the \(x\)-axis sits at height zero, so its second coordinate is \(0\). Set the second entry of the pair equal to \(0\).
That gives \(c+12=0\), a one-step equation. The first entry is not needed at all.
review.sol: A point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y\)-coordinate \(0\), so \(c+12=0\) and \(c=\boxed{-12}\). The point is then \((-7,0)\). Setting the first entry to zero instead gives \(c=-5\), which puts the point on the \(y\)-axis rather than the \(x\)-axis.

review.x: Enter the distance between \((-8,-6)\) and \((15,-6)\).
hints: Both points sit at the same height, \(y=-6\), so the segment joining them is horizontal and only the \(x\)-coordinates differ.
The gap is the larger \(x\)-coordinate minus the smaller, \(15-(-8)\), and subtracting a negative is the same as adding.
review.sol: Both points have \(y=-6\), so the segment is horizontal and the distance is \(15-(-8)=15+8=\boxed{23}\). When two points share a coordinate, only the other pair of coordinates matters, and the distance is the larger minus the smaller.

review.x: Enter the distance between \((7,-21)\) and \((7,9)\).
hints: The two points share their \(x\)-coordinate, so the segment joining them is vertical and only the heights differ.
Subtract the lower \(y\)-coordinate from the upper one, and take care with the sign, since the number being subtracted is negative.
review.sol: Both points have \(x=7\), so the distance is \(9-(-21)=9+21=\boxed{30}\). A shared \(x\)-coordinate means a vertical segment, and a shared \(y\)-coordinate means a horizontal one.

review.x: Enter the distance between \((2,-3)\) and \((26,4)\).
hints: The two points share no coordinate, so the distance cannot be found by one subtraction and the full formula is needed. It is built from the difference of the \(x\)-coordinates and the difference of the \(y\)-coordinates.
The two differences are \(24\) and \(7\). Square each, add, then take the square root.
review.sol: The differences are \(26-2=24\) and \(4-(-3)=7\), so the distance is \(\sqrt{24^2+7^2}=\sqrt{576+49}=\sqrt{625}=\boxed{25}\). Reading \(4-(-3)\) as \(1\) is the usual slip, and it gives \(\sqrt{577}\) instead.

review.x: Enter the distance from the origin to the point \((-9,-40)\).
hints: The origin is \((0,0)\), so each difference in the distance formula is just one of the point's own coordinates.
A negative squared is positive, so the sum under the radical is \(9^2+40^2\), and that total is a perfect square.
review.sol: Taking \((x_1,y_1)=(0,0)\), the differences are \(-9\) and \(-40\), so the distance is \(\sqrt{(-9)^2+(-40)^2}=\sqrt{81+1600}=\sqrt{1681}=\boxed{41}\). With the origin as the first point, \(x_1\) and \(y_1\) are both zero, so the legs of the right triangle have lengths \(9\) and \(40\), the sizes of the point's own coordinates.

review.x: The distance between \((-5,3)\) and \((4,21)\) simplifies to \(a\sqrt{5}\), where \(a\) is a whole number. Enter \(a\).
hints: Take the two differences \(4-(-5)\) and \(21-3\), square each one and add. Watch the double negative in the first difference.
The sum under the radical is \(405\), and \(405=81\cdot 5\). Chapter 3 covered simplifying a radical, which means taking the square root of the perfect square factor and leaving the rest inside.
review.sol: The differences are \(4-(-5)=9\) and \(21-3=18\), so the distance is \(\sqrt{9^2+18^2}=\sqrt{81+324}=\sqrt{405}\). Since \(405=81\cdot 5\), that is \(\sqrt{81}\sqrt{5}=9\sqrt{5}\), so \(a=\boxed{9}\). Splitting \(405\) as \(9\cdot 45\) gives \(3\sqrt{45}\), the same number in a form that is not simplified, so take the largest perfect square factor, \(81\).

review.x: Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the midpoint of the segment joining \((-13,-20)\) and \((49,6)\).
hints: The midpoint's \(x\)-coordinate is the average of the two \(x\)-coordinates, so the two \(y\)-coordinates are not needed for it.
Average \(-13\) and \(49\) by adding them first and then halving.
review.sol: The \(x\)-coordinates average to \(\frac{-13+49}{2}=\frac{36}{2}=\boxed{18}\). Each coordinate of the midpoint is averaged on its own, so the \(-20\) and the \(6\) are used only for the midpoint's \(y\)-coordinate, which is \(-7\).

review.x: Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the midpoint of the segment joining \((6,-3)\) and \((20,10)\).
hints: The midpoint's \(y\)-coordinate is the average of \(-3\) and \(10\), so the two \(x\)-coordinates are not needed here.
Add \(-3\) and \(10\), then halve. The sum is odd, so the answer is not a whole number.
review.sol: The \(y\)-coordinates average to \(\frac{-3+10}{2}=\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\). With whole-number coordinates, the average is a whole number only when the two are both even or both odd, so a fraction here is correct rather than a sign of a slip.

review.x: The segment with endpoints \(P=(-7,3)\) and \(Q\) has midpoint \((4,-6)\). Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of \(Q\).
hints: The midpoint's \(x\)-coordinate is the average of the two endpoints' \(x\)-coordinates, and here the average is known while one of the two numbers being averaged is not.
Let \(q\) stand for the \(x\)-coordinate of \(Q\), so \(\frac{-7+q}{2}=4\). Multiplying both sides by \(2\) clears the fraction first.
review.sol: Writing \(Q=(q,r)\), the \(x\)-coordinates average to \(4\), so \(\frac{-7+q}{2}=4\), giving \(-7+q=8\) and \(q=\boxed{15}\). As a check, \(-7\) to \(4\) is a step of \(11\), and \(4+11=15\).

review.x: The midpoint of the segment joining \((-31,4)\) and \((t,10)\) lies on the \(y\)-axis. Enter \(t\).
hints: A point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x\)-coordinate \(0\), so the midpoint's first coordinate is known even though the midpoint itself is not given.
The two \(x\)-coordinates average to \(0\), so \(\frac{-31+t}{2}=0\). The \(y\)-coordinates \(4\) and \(10\) are not needed.
review.sol: A point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x\)-coordinate \(0\), so \(\frac{-31+t}{2}=0\), giving \(-31+t=0\) and \(t=\boxed{31}\). The \(y\)-axis is the line \(x=0\), not \(y=0\), so only the first coordinates matter here. Averaging \(4\) and \(10\) instead gives \(7\) for every \(t\), so that reading has no solution.

review.x: A segment has one endpoint at \((-6,1)\) and its midpoint at \((14,22)\). Enter the length of the whole segment.
hints: The midpoint is halfway along, so the distance from it to an endpoint is half the whole length, and both of those points are given.
The differences from \((-6,1)\) to \((14,22)\) are \(20\) and \(21\). Those are the legs of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is half the segment, so double what you get.
review.sol: The differences from \((-6,1)\) to \((14,22)\) are \(20\) and \(21\), so half the segment is \(\sqrt{20^2+21^2}=\sqrt{400+441}=\sqrt{841}=29\) and the whole segment is \(\boxed{58}\). Working the long way gives the same number. The other endpoint is \((34,43)\), and \(\sqrt{40^2+42^2}=\sqrt{3364}=58\).

blocks.x: 7.1 gave every ordered pair a place on the plane. From 5.1, an equation in two variables has one solution pair for every value of \(x\) chosen, so its solutions can never be listed in full. Every one of those pairs is a point. Marking all of them at once replaces the endless list with one picture.

The graph of \(3x+4y=29\) is the set of points whose coordinates make that equation true. One of \((7,2)\) and \((9,1)\) is on the graph and the other is not. Substitute both, and enter the value the left side takes at the point that is not on the graph.
hints: Substituting a point puts its first coordinate in for \(x\) and its second for \(y\), then evaluates \(3x+4y\). Do that for both points and compare each result with \(29\).
Start with \((7,2)\). If \(3(7)+4(2)\) comes out to \(29\), that point is on the graph, and the value you want is whatever \(3x+4y\) gives at \((9,1)\).
blocks.sol: Substituting \((9,1)\) into the left side gives \(3(9)+4(1)=27+4=\boxed{31}\). The other point does satisfy the equation, since \(3(7)+4(2)=21+8=29\), so \((7,2)\) is on the graph and \((9,1)\), where the left side comes out to \(31\) instead of \(29\), is not.

blocks.x: The notation \((x,8)\) means a point whose second coordinate is \(8\) and whose first coordinate is not yet known. That point is on the graph of \(5x-3y=11\). Enter its \(x\)-coordinate.
hints: The number given is the second coordinate, so it is the value of \(y\). Substitute it and the equation has only \(x\) left in it.
The equation becomes \(5x-24=11\).
blocks.sol: Substituting \(y=8\) gives \(5x-3(8)=11\), which is \(5x-24=11\). Then \(5x=35\) and \(x=\boxed{7}\). A point is on the graph exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation, so the known coordinate goes in for its own letter and the missing one is left to solve for.

blocks.x: The graph of an equation is the set of its solution points. Every solution pair \((x,y)\) is one point, and the graph of the equation is the collection of exactly those points and no others. A point is on the graph when substituting its two coordinates makes the equation true, and off the graph otherwise, which is 5.1's check with the pair read as a point. The test is arithmetic and not appearance. A point with fractional coordinates is on the graph whenever its substitution is true, and a point drawn close by is off the graph whenever its substitution is false.

Build a table for \(3x+2y=30\) at \(x=0,\ 2,\ 4,\ 6,\ 8\), solving for \(y\) in each row. The five pairs all lie on one straight line, and exactly one of them has its two coordinates equal. Enter the value those two coordinates share.
hints: Each row takes one value of \(x\) and solves \(3x+2y=30\) for \(y\), so the row for \(x=2\) reads \(6+2y=30\).
A row with equal coordinates has \(y\) equal to its own \(x\), so replacing \(y\) with \(x\) in \(3x+2y=30\) turns it into an equation in \(x\) alone.
blocks.sol: The rows give \((0,15)\), \((2,12)\), \((4,9)\), \((6,6)\) and \((8,3)\), and the pair with equal coordinates is \((6,6)\), so the shared value is \(\boxed{6}\). All five pairs satisfy the equation, so all five are points of the same line, and any two of them are enough to draw it.

blocks.x: Exactly one of these four points is not on the graph of \(4x-3y=18\). $$\left(\tfrac{3}{4},-5\right)\qquad(3,-2)\qquad(9,7)\qquad(12,10)$$ Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point that is not.
hints: Test all four the same way, including the one with a fractional coordinate. A fraction is a perfectly good coordinate, and all that matters is whether \(4x-3y\) comes out to \(18\).
Watch the signs. At \(\left(\tfrac34,-5\right)\) the term \(-3y\) becomes \(+15\), and at \((3,-2)\) it becomes \(+6\).
blocks.sol: The four left sides are \(3+15=18\), \(12+6=18\), \(36-21=15\) and \(48-30=18\). Only \((9,7)\) gives something other than \(18\), and its \(x\)-coordinate is \(\boxed{9}\). Whether a point is on the graph depends only on what the substitution gives, not on how tidy the coordinates look, so here the fractional point is on the line and a whole-number point is not.

blocks.x: The graph of \(ax+by=c\) is a straight line. Whenever \(a\) and \(b\) are not both zero, the points that satisfy \(ax+by=c\) all lie in one straight line, and every point of that line satisfies the equation. An equation of this form is a linear equation in two variables, named for that line. Through two distinct points there is exactly one straight line, so two solution pairs are enough to draw the whole graph, however many solutions the equation has in total.
