blocks.cap: Each marked point satisfies \(x+2y=10\), and the substitution under it is the whole test. The graph is every point that passes, and those points fall in one straight line that continues past the three marked here.

blocks.x: Two points are enough to draw the line, so a third pair is spare, and a spare point is a check. Any two points lie in a straight line, even two computed wrongly, so an arithmetic slip is invisible with only two points. Three points in one line is a condition that can fail, so a third point off the line is proof that one of the three is wrong.
The point \((4,2)\) is on the graph of \(7x-ky=6\), where \(k\) is a constant. Only one value of \(k\) makes that true. Enter \(k\).
hints: Testing a point is the same substitution whether the unknown is a coordinate or a coefficient. Putting both coordinates in leaves an equation whose only unknown is \(k\).
With \(x=4\) and \(y=2\) the equation reads \(28-2k=6\). Note the minus sign in front of the \(k\) term.
blocks.sol: Substituting gives \(7(4)-k(2)=6\), so \(28-2k=6\), then \(2k=22\) and \(k=\boxed{11}\). Check, \(7(4)-11(2)=28-22=6\). The usual slip is reading \(-k(2)\) as \(+2k\), which gives \(28+2k=6\) and \(k=-11\).

blocks.x: A student computes three pairs for \(2x+5y=34\) and gets \((2,6)\), \((7,4)\) and \((12,3)\). Plotted, the three points do not fall in a straight line, so one pair is wrong. Keep the \(x\)-value of the pair that fails, and enter the \(y\)-value that belongs with it.
hints: Two of the three pairs satisfy the equation and one does not, so run the test on all three before deciding which one to fix.
The three left sides come out \(34\), \(34\) and \(39\). Take the \(x\)-value of the pair that misses and solve \(2x+5y=34\) for \(y\) again.
blocks.sol: The three left sides are \(4+30=34\), \(14+20=34\) and \(24+15=39\), so \((12,3)\) is the wrong pair. At \(x=12\), \(5y=34-24=10\) and \(y=\boxed{2}\). The corrected point sits one unit below the plotted one, which is why the three looked nearly straight rather than obviously wrong. A third point is worth computing for exactly that reason.

blocks.x: Plot from a table, then check with a third point. Choose a value of \(x\), substitute it into the equation, and solve for \(y\). Each row of the table is one solution pair and so one point, and two rows are enough to draw the line. The point from a third row is on that same line when all three pairs are right and off it when one of them is wrong, so a third row is worth computing before the line is drawn rather than after. Choosing values of \(x\) for which \(y\) is a whole number keeps every point easy to plot.

Any value of \(x\) is allowed in the table, and two choices take less work than the rest. Where a graph crosses an axis, one coordinate is already known, so only the other is left to compute. The next two problems find those crossings, and a later pair shows that a graph need not cross both axes at all.
The graph of \(3x+8y=24\) is a straight line, and it meets the \(x\)-axis at exactly one point. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of that point.
hints: Every point of the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), which 7.1 established. That is the value to substitute here.
With \(y=0\) the term \(8y\) is \(0\), so the equation becomes \(3x=24\).
blocks.sol: A point of the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so \(3x+8(0)=24\), which is \(3x=24\), and \(x=\boxed{8}\). Setting \(x=0\) instead gives \(8y=24\) and \(y=3\), the crossing on the \(y\)-axis rather than the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.x: William Playfair published the first line graphs of economic data in 1786, in his Commercial and Political Atlas. He put time along the bottom and money up the side, so a trend could be seen rather than read from a table.
The graph of \(3x-4y=48\) is a straight line that crosses the \(y\)-axis once. Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the crossing point.
hints: Every point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\), so substitute that value and solve for \(y\).
The equation becomes \(-4y=48\), and the coefficient of \(y\) is negative, so divide both sides by \(-4\) and keep the sign.
blocks.sol: A point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\), so \(3(0)-4y=48\), which is \(-4y=48\), and \(y=\boxed{-12}\). Dropping the minus gives \(12\) and puts the crossing above the origin instead of below it, and setting \(y=0\) by mistake gives \(16\), which is the \(x\)-axis crossing.

blocks.x: The intercepts. The \(x\)-intercept is where a graph meets the \(x\)-axis, and every point of that axis has \(y=0\), so substituting \(y=0\) gives it. The \(y\)-intercept is where the graph meets the \(y\)-axis, and every point there has \(x=0\), so substituting \(x=0\) gives it. The row \((0,15)\) in the table for \(3x+2y=30\) has \(x=0\), so it was that graph's \(y\)-intercept all along. Each substitution leaves a one-letter equation, so the intercepts are the two cheapest points to plot. The variable set to zero is never the one the intercept is named after.

Every equation so far has had both letters in it. In \(ax+by=c\) only one of \(a\) and \(b\) has to be nonzero, so the other may be zero. With \(a=0\) what remains is \(by=c\), and dividing by \(b\) leaves \(y=k\). With \(b=0\) what remains is \(x=k\). Each still has a graph, and the next two problems settle which points are on it.
In the coordinate plane, the graph of \(2y+9=-5\) is made of exactly the points \((x,y)\) that satisfy it. One of those points has first coordinate \(40\). Enter that point's second coordinate.
hints: The equation contains no \(x\), so the first coordinate can be anything at all. The only condition is on the second coordinate.
Solve \(2y+9=-5\) for \(y\) the same way you would solve any one-variable equation. The \(40\) is not needed for that work.
blocks.sol: From \(2y+9=-5\), \(2y=-14\) and \(y=\boxed{-7}\). Because the equation contains no \(x\), every point on this graph has second coordinate \(-7\), whatever the first coordinate is. That is why the \(40\) is not needed.

blocks.x: The graph of \(3x=-18\) is a straight line. Enter the number of points that line has in common with the \(y\)-axis.
hints: Solve for \(x\) first, then describe the graph. No \(y\) appears, so every point of the graph shares one \(x\)-coordinate.
From 7.1, a point is on the \(y\)-axis exactly when its \(x\)-coordinate is \(0\). Compare that with the \(x\)-coordinate every point of this graph has.
blocks.sol: Solving gives \(x=-6\), so every point of the graph has first coordinate \(-6\). A point of the \(y\)-axis has first coordinate \(0\), and \(-6 eq 0\), so the number of shared points is \(\boxed{0}\). Reading \(x=-6\) as a horizontal line gives the answer \(1\) instead, since a horizontal line does meet the \(y\)-axis once.

blocks.x: \(y=k\) is a horizontal line and \(x=k\) is a vertical line. A point satisfies \(y=k\) exactly when its second coordinate is \(k\), with no condition on its first, so the graph is every point at height \(k\), which is a horizontal line. A point satisfies \(x=k\) exactly when its first coordinate is \(k\), with none on its second, so the graph is the vertical line through \((k,0)\). The letter in the equation is the fixed coordinate, not the direction of the line. So \(x=k\) has no \(y\)-intercept unless \(k=0\), since every point of the \(y\)-axis has first coordinate \(0\).

The last two problems use every piece at once. An equation is not always written in the form \(ax+by=c\), and terms in the same letter may appear on both sides, so collecting them onto one side comes first. A coefficient can also be unknown, and then one stated fact about the graph is enough to determine it.
The graph of \(9y-4x=30+5y\) is a straight line. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point where it meets the \(x\)-axis.
hints: The \(y\) terms sit on both sides. Collect them on one side first, and the equation takes the form \(ax+by=c\).
Collecting gives \(4y-4x=30\). Every point of the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so put that value in and solve for \(x\).
blocks.sol: Subtracting \(5y\) from both sides gives \(4y-4x=30\). A point of the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so \(-4x=30\) and \(x=\boxed{-\frac{15}{2}}\). Setting \(x=0\) instead gives \(4y=30\) and \(y=\frac{15}{2}\), which is where the line meets the \(y\)-axis, not the \(x\)-axis.

blocks.x: The graph of \(6x+by=21\) has no point in common with the \(y\)-axis, where \(b\) is a constant. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point on that graph whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(-11\).
hints: Substituting \(y=-11\) straight away leaves two unknowns, so use the stated fact first. A point sits on the \(y\)-axis exactly when its \(x\)-coordinate is \(0\), so put \(x=0\) into the equation.
If \(b eq0\), then \(x=0\) gives \(by=21\) and a point on the \(y\)-axis exists. The graph has no such point, so only one value of \(b\) is possible, and the equation is left with no \(y\) term.
blocks.sol: If \(b eq 0\), setting \(x=0\) gives \(by=21\) and a point on the \(y\)-axis. The graph has no such point, so \(b=0\) and the equation is \(6x=21\). Every point of that graph has \(x=\frac{21}{6}\), so the one with \(y=-11\) has \(x=\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\). The form \(ax+by=c\) allows \(b=0\) as long as \(a\) is not zero too, and here \(a=6\). With \(b=0\) the equation contains no \(y\), so the \(-11\) is not needed.

blocks.x: Every graph in this lesson came from the same two steps, find two solution points and draw the line through them. Those steps settle where the line is and say nothing about how steep it is. Lesson 7.3, Slope, attaches a number to the steepness, computed from any two points of the line.

review.x: Substitute the point \((6,3)\) into the left side of \(2x+3y=19\), and enter the resulting value of \(2x+3y\).
hints: In \((6,3)\) the first coordinate is the \(x\)-value and the second is the \(y\)-value, so substitute \(6\) for \(x\) and \(3\) for \(y\) in \(2x+3y\).
Work out \(2\times 6\) and \(3\times 3\) as separate terms before adding them. The total need not be \(19\), since only points on the graph make the left side equal \(19\).
review.sol: Substituting gives \(2(6)+3(3)=12+9=\boxed{21}\). The left side comes out \(21\) while the right side is \(19\), so \((6,3)\) does not satisfy the equation and does not lie on the graph.

review.x: The point \((4,y)\) is on the graph of \(x+y=17\). Enter \(y\).
hints: The \(4\) is the first coordinate, so it is the value of \(x\), and the second coordinate is what remains to be found.
The equation becomes \(4+y=17\).
review.sol: The point has \(x=4\), so \(4+y=17\) and \(y=\boxed{13}\). A point is on the graph exactly when its two coordinates make the equation true, so putting in the coordinate that is given leaves one equation in one unknown.

review.x: The point \((x,3)\) is on the graph of \(5x-2y=64\). Enter the value of \(x\).
hints: The \(3\) is the second coordinate, so it goes in for \(y\), not for \(x\).
With \(y=3\) the equation reads \(5x-6=64\).
review.sol: The point has \(y=3\), so \(5x-2(3)=64\), which is \(5x-6=64\). Then \(5x=70\) and \(x=\boxed{14}\). Check, \(5(14)-2(3)=70-6=64\). Putting the \(3\) in for \(x\) instead gives \(15-2y=64\), a different point on the same line.

review.x: The graph of \(9x+2y=-8\) contains a point whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(-2\). Enter that point's \(y\)-coordinate.
hints: A point lies on the graph exactly when its coordinates make the equation true, so \((-2,y)\) has to satisfy \(9x+2y=-8\).
Substituting gives \(9(-2)=-18\), not \(18\), so the equation to solve is \(-18+2y=-8\).
review.sol: Substituting \(x=-2\) gives \(9(-2)+2y=-8\), so \(-18+2y=-8\), then \(2y=10\) and \(y=\boxed{5}\). Dropping the negative gives \(18+2y=-8\) and \(y=-13\), the common wrong answer.

review.x: Three of \((5,13)\), \((8,7)\), \((10,4)\), \((1,21)\) are on the graph of \(2x+y=23\) and one is not. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the one that is not.
hints: Evaluate \(2x+y\) at each of the four and compare each result with \(23\).
Three of the four give \(23\) and one gives \(24\).
review.sol: Substituting gives \(10+13=23\), \(16+7=23\), \(20+4=24\) and \(2+21=23\). The third value is not \(23\), so the point off the graph is \((10,4)\) and the answer is \(\boxed{10}\). A point is on the graph exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation, so one failed check is enough to rule a point out.

review.x: Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point where the graph of \(5x+2y=60\) meets the \(x\)-axis.
hints: Every point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so that is the value to substitute.
Watch which zero goes in. Substituting \(x=0\) instead leads to the point where the graph meets the \(y\)-axis, which is not what is asked.
review.sol: Every point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so \(5x+2(0)=60\), which is \(5x=60\), and \(x=\boxed{12}\). Reversing the substitution and setting \(x=0\) gives \(2y=60\) and \(y=30\), which is the \(y\)-coordinate of the point where the graph meets the \(y\)-axis.

review.x: Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point where the graph of \(7x-3y=42\) meets the \(y\)-axis.
hints: Every point on the \(y\)-axis has first coordinate \(0\), so that is the value to substitute into \(7x-3y=42\).
Substituting leaves \(-3y=42\), where the coefficient of \(y\) is negative. Dividing a positive number by a negative one gives a negative result, so a positive answer here means a sign was dropped.
review.sol: Every point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\), so \(7(0)-3y=42\), which is \(-3y=42\), and \(y=\boxed{-14}\). Setting \(y=0\) instead gives \(7x=42\) and the number \(6\), which is where the graph meets the \(x\)-axis, not the \(y\)-axis.

review.x: A point on the graph of \(5y+31=6\) has first coordinate \(-90\). Enter its second coordinate.
hints: The equation contains no \(x\), so whether a point satisfies it depends only on the second coordinate.
Subtract \(31\) from both sides, then divide by \(5\).
review.sol: From \(5y+31=6\), \(5y=-25\) and \(y=\boxed{-5}\). The equation contains no \(x\), so every point of this graph has second coordinate \(-5\) whatever its first coordinate is, which makes the \(-90\) irrelevant.

review.x: In the coordinate plane, the graph of \(4x+29=5\) contains a point whose second coordinate is \(41\). Enter that point's first coordinate.
hints: The equation has no \(y\) in it, so every point of the graph has the same first coordinate.
Solve \(4x+29=5\) by itself, since \(41\) is not part of that equation.
review.sol: From \(4x+29=5\), subtracting \(29\) gives \(4x=-24\), so \(x=\boxed{-6}\). The equation has no \(y\) in it, so every point of the graph has first coordinate \(-6\) whatever its second coordinate is, and the graph is the vertical line \(x=-6\). The \(41\) is not needed.

review.x: The point \((2,5)\) is on the graph of \(kx-4y=10\), where \(k\) is a constant. Enter \(k\).
hints: A point is on the graph when substituting its coordinates makes the equation true, and here that substitution leaves \(k\) as the only unknown.
Putting in \(x=2\) and \(y=5\), the equation reads \(2k-20=10\).
review.sol: Substituting gives \(k(2)-4(5)=10\), so \(2k-20=10\), then \(2k=30\) and \(k=\boxed{15}\). Checking it back, \(15(2)-4(5)=30-20=10\), so \((2,5)\) does satisfy the equation with that value of \(k\).

review.x: Enter the \(y\)-coordinate, exactly, of the point where the graph of \(8x+5y=18\) meets the \(y\)-axis.
hints: Every point of the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\), so substitute that into \(8x+5y=18\) and solve for what is left.
The equation becomes \(5y=18\), and \(18\) is not a multiple of \(5\), so the answer is a fraction.
review.sol: A point of the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\), so \(8(0)+5y=18\), which is \(5y=18\), and \(y=\boxed{\frac{18}{5}}\). The crossing point is not required to have a whole-number coordinate, so keep the fraction in lowest terms rather than rounding it.

review.x: The graph of \(9x=20-2y\) crosses the \(x\)-axis at exactly one point. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of that point as an exact fraction.
hints: Every point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so put \(0\) in for \(y\) and see what the equation then says about \(x\).
There is no need to rearrange the equation first. With \(y=0\) the right side is \(20-2(0)\), and a single division then isolates \(x\).
review.sol: Every point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so the equation becomes \(9x=20-2(0)=20\), and dividing by \(9\) gives \(x=\boxed{\frac{20}{9}}\). Since \(20\) is not a multiple of \(9\), the exact coordinate is that fraction, and a rounded decimal does not satisfy the equation.

review.x: A student lists \((5,9)\), \((10,6)\) and \((15,4)\) as points on the graph of \(3x+5y=60\). Plotted, the three do not fall in a straight line, so one pair is wrong. Keeping that pair's \(x\)-value, enter the correct \(y\)-value.
hints: A pair is on the graph exactly when substituting its two coordinates makes \(3x+5y=60\) true. Run that test on all three before deciding which one to fix.
The three left sides come out \(60\), \(60\) and \(65\). Take the \(x\)-value of the pair that does not give \(60\) and solve \(3x+5y=60\) for \(y\) again.
review.sol: The three left sides are \(15+45=60\), \(30+30=60\) and \(45+20=65\), so \((15,4)\) is the wrong pair. At \(x=15\), \(5y=60-45=15\) and \(y=\boxed{3}\). Two points always fall in one straight line, wrong ones included, so a bad pair only shows up once a third point is plotted.

review.x: Enter the number of distinct points where the graph of \(4x-7y=0\) meets an axis.
hints: A point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), and a point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\). Do the two substitutions separately and write down the coordinates each one gives.
Setting \(y=0\) leaves \(4x=0\), and setting \(x=0\) leaves \(-7y=0\). Solve both, write out both points in full, then compare them before you count.
review.sol: Both crossings are the same point, the origin, so the answer is \(\boxed{1}\). Setting \(y=0\) gives \(4x=0\) and so \(x=0\), and setting \(x=0\) gives \(-7y=0\) and so \(y=0\), which makes both crossings \((0,0)\). Counting one crossing per axis gives \(2\) and counts the origin twice.

review.x: Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point where the graph of \(3(x-y)=x+38\) meets the \(x\)-axis.
hints: A point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), and that substitution can be made before anything is expanded.
With \(y=0\) the equation reads \(3x=x+38\), and the \(x\) terms sit on both sides.
review.sol: A point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), so \(3(x-0)=x+38\), which is \(3x=x+38\). Subtracting \(x\) from both sides gives \(2x=38\), so \(x=\boxed{19}\). Setting \(x=0\) instead finds where the graph meets the \(y\)-axis, a different point. Check, \(3(19-0)=57\) and \(19+38=57\).

review.x: The graph of \(px+8y=20\) has no point in common with the \(x\)-axis, where \(p\) is a constant. Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that graph whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(-25\).
hints: Substituting \(x=-25\) first leaves two unknowns, so use the stated fact instead. A point on the \(x\)-axis is a point with \(y=0\), so set \(y=0\) in \(px+8y=20\) and see what is left.

With \(y=0\) the equation reads \(px=20\). If \(p\) is not zero, that equation has the solution \(x=\frac{20}{p}\), which would put a point of the graph on the \(x\)-axis. Only one value of \(p\) is left, so put it back into the original equation.
review.sol: A point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\), and the equation then reads \(px=20\). If \(p eq 0\) this gives the point \(\left(\frac{20}{p},0\right)\) on the \(x\)-axis, so \(p=0\) and the equation is \(8y=20\). Every point of the graph has \(y=\frac{20}{8}\), so the point with \(x=-25\) has \(y=\boxed{\frac{5}{2}}\). With \(p=0\) the graph is the horizontal line \(y=\frac{5}{2}\), so the \(x\)-coordinate does not matter here.

review.x: The graph of \(8y-15x=120\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \(A\) and the \(y\)-axis at \(B\). Enter the distance between \(A\) and \(B\).
hints: Find both crossings first, one substitution each, and write each one as a point before doing any distance work.
The two points are \((-8,0)\) and \((0,15)\). Use the distance formula from 7.1, \(\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\).
review.sol: Setting \(y=0\) gives \(-15x=120\), so \(x=-8\) and \(A=(-8,0)\). Setting \(x=0\) gives \(8y=120\), so \(y=15\) and \(B=(0,15)\). Then the distance is \(\sqrt{(-8-0)^2+(0-15)^2}=\sqrt{64+225}=\sqrt{289}=\boxed{17}\). Each crossing sits on an axis, so the horizontal gap is \(8\) and the vertical gap is \(15\), and \(8^2+15^2=17^2\) is why the distance comes out whole.

blocks.x: Where a line is and how steep it is are two different questions, and 7.2 answered only the first. Steepness is a comparison of two changes, how much \(y\) changes from one point of a line to another and how much \(x\) changes between the same two points. Both are subtractions of coordinates, so any two points are enough to make the comparison.

A line passes through \((2,5)\) and \((6,17)\). Going from the first point to the second, find how much \(y\) changes and how much \(x\) changes, then enter the value of the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\).
hints: Each change is a subtraction, the second point's coordinate minus the first point's. For \(y\) that is \(17-5\).
The change in \(y\) is \(12\) and the change in \(x\) is \(6-2\). Divide the first by the second.
blocks.sol: The change in \(y\) is \(17-5=12\) and the change in \(x\) is \(6-2=4\), so the quotient is \(\frac{12}{4}=\boxed{3}\). A quotient of \(3\) means \(y\) changes by \(3\) for every \(1\) that \(x\) changes.

blocks.x: Three more points are claimed to lie on that same line, \((-1,-4)\), \((5,14)\) and \((9,25)\). From \((2,5)\) to each of them, compute the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\). Two of the three quotients come out \(3\), the value from the previous problem, and one does not. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point whose quotient is not \(3\).
hints: Run the same two subtractions three times, always starting from \((2,5)\), and compare each quotient with \(3\).
From \((2,5)\) to \((-1,-4)\) both changes are negative, \(-9\) and \(-3\), and a negative divided by a negative is positive. Check the other two the same way.
blocks.sol: From \((2,5)\) the quotient to \((-1,-4)\) is \(\frac{-9}{-3}=3\), the quotient to \((5,14)\) is \(\frac{9}{3}=3\), and the quotient to \((9,25)\) is \(\frac{20}{7}\). Only the third differs from \(3\), so the \(x\)-coordinate asked for is \(\boxed{9}\). Two different second points on the line both give \(3\), so the quotient does not depend on which pair is used. The one point that gives something else is off the line.

blocks.x: The slope of a line. For two points \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\) of a line, the slope of that line is $$m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1},$$ the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\), and \(m\) is the standard letter for it. Every pair of points of one line gives the same value, which is why three different pairs above all gave \(3\), and the pair that gave something else used a point off the line. A slope is a property of the whole line, so any two of its points are enough to compute it.
A line passes through \((-4,9)\) and \((2,-9)\). Enter its slope.
hints: Take \((-4,9)\) first in both subtractions. The change in \(y\) is then \(-9-9\).
The change in \(y\) is \(-18\) and the change in \(x\) is \(2-(-4)=6\).
blocks.sol: Taking \((-4,9)\) first, \(m=\frac{-9-9}{2-(-4)}=\frac{-18}{6}=\boxed{-3}\). Between these points \(y\) decreases while \(x\) increases, so the top of the fraction is negative, the bottom is positive, and the slope is negative.

blocks.x: A line passes through \((3,-4)\) and \((9,8)\). A student writes \(\frac{-4-8}{9-3}\) and reports \(-2\), subtracting the \(y\)-values in one order and the \(x\)-values in the other order. Enter the correct slope.
hints: Both differences have to be taken in the same order, so pick one point to come first and use that point first on the top and on the bottom.
With \((9,8)\) first in both, the top is \(8-(-4)\) and the bottom is \(9-3\).
blocks.sol: With \((9,8)\) first in both differences, \(m=\frac{8-(-4)}{9-3}=\frac{12}{6}=\boxed{2}\). The student's \(-2\) has the right size and the wrong sign, because only the top was reversed, and a reversed top is the negative of the correct top.

blocks.x: Keep the same point first in both subtractions. Either of the two points may be written first, but the choice on the top and the choice on the bottom have to match. Taking the other point first reverses the sign of \(y_2-y_1\) and of \(x_2-x_1\) at once, and the two reversals cancel, so \(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\) and \(\frac{y_1-y_2}{x_1-x_2}\) are the same number. Mixing the two orders reverses the sign of just one of them, so the result is the negative of the slope. That is where \(-2\) came from for a line of slope \(2\), the right size with the wrong sign.

blocks.cap: The same line, with a slope triangle drawn under two different stretches of it. As the triangle slides along and changes size, the run and the rise change together, so the quotient \(\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}\) is the same wherever it is measured. That is why any two points of a line give the same slope.

blocks.x: Writing the left-hand point first makes the change in \(x\) positive, since the other point has the larger \(x\). The sign of the quotient then depends only on the change in \(y\), positive when the right-hand point is higher and negative when it is lower. So the sign of a slope follows from where two points are, with no coordinates needed.

Points \(P\) and \(Q\) lie on the same line, with \(Q\) to the right of \(P\) and lower than \(P\). No coordinates are given, so no number can be computed for the slope of that line, but its sign can be named. Enter the word positive or negative.
hints: Take \(P\) first in both subtractions. \(Q\) is to the right of \(P\), so the change in \(x\) is positive.
\(Q\) is lower than \(P\), so the change in \(y\) is a negative number while the change in \(x\) stays positive. Think about the sign of a fraction whose top and bottom have opposite signs.
blocks.sol: Taking \(P\) first, the change in \(x\) is positive because \(Q\) is to the right, and the change in \(y\) is negative because \(Q\) is lower, so the slope is \(\boxed{\text{negative}}\). Taking \(Q\) first flips the sign of both changes, so the quotient is negative either way.

blocks.x: A line passes through \((-6,-5)\) and \((10,7)\). Enter its slope as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Take \((-6,-5)\) as the first point and subtract in that same order on the top and the bottom. Both differences involve subtracting a negative number.
The top and the bottom share a common factor, so the fraction you get first is not in lowest terms. Divide both by that factor.
blocks.sol: Taking \((-6,-5)\) first, \(m=\frac{7-(-5)}{10-(-6)}=\frac{12}{16}=\boxed{\frac{3}{4}}\). Both differences are positive because the second point is above and to the right of the first. Stopping at \(\frac{12}{16}\) is the common miss, since the answer was asked for in lowest terms.

blocks.x: The sign of \(m\) gives the direction and \(|m|\) gives the steepness. A line with \(m>0\) rises from left to right, a line with \(m<0\) falls from left to right, and \(m=0\) means every point of the line has the same \(y\), so the line is horizontal. The number \(|m|\) is how much \(y\) changes across one unit of change in \(x\), so \(|m|=4\) is a change of four units and \(|m|=\frac{1}{4}\) is a change of a quarter of a unit. Steepness is measured by \(|m|\) and not by \(m\), so a slope of \(-4\) is steeper than a slope of \(3\).

Two kinds of line from 7.2 have not been put through the definition, the horizontal and the vertical. Every point of a horizontal line has the same \(y\) and every point of a vertical line has the same \(x\), so one of the two changes is \(0\) in each case. A \(0\) on top and a \(0\) underneath are not the same, as the next two problems show.
From 7.2 the graph of \(y=6\) is a horizontal line, and \((-8,6)\) and \((15,6)\) are two of its points. Enter its slope, or the word undefined if it has none.
hints: The two points have the same second coordinate, so start with the change in \(y\).
The change in \(y\) is \(6-6\) and the change in \(x\) is \(15-(-8)\). Work both out, then divide the change in \(y\) by the change in \(x\).
blocks.sol: The change in \(y\) is \(6-6=0\) and the change in \(x\) is \(15-(-8)=23\), so \(m=\frac{0}{23}=\boxed{0}\). Zero divided by a nonzero number is \(0\), so every horizontal line has slope \(0\), however far apart its two points are.

blocks.x: Gaspard Monge set out descriptive geometry around 1795, pinning a solid object down by its projections onto two perpendicular planes. France kept it a military secret for years before it was taught at the Ecole Polytechnique.
From 7.2 the graph of \(x=-3\) is a vertical line, and \((-3,4)\) and \((-3,-9)\) are two of its points. Enter its slope, or the word undefined if it has none.
hints: The two points have the same first coordinate, so look at the bottom of the fraction before the top.
The change in \(y\) is \(-9-4=-13\) and the change in \(x\) is \(-3-(-3)=0\). Ask what number multiplied by \(0\) gives \(-13\).
blocks.sol: The change in \(y\) is \(-9-4=-13\) and the change in \(x\) is \(-3-(-3)=0\), so the slope would be \(\frac{-13}{0}\), and division by zero has no value. The slope is \(\boxed{\text{undefined}}\). Answering \(0\) is the standard slip. A slope of \(0\) is a number and belongs to a horizontal line, while a vertical line has no slope at all.

blocks.x: A vertical line has no slope, and that is not the same as a slope of \(0\). Two points of a vertical line have the same \(x\), so \(x_2-x_1=0\), and the quotient is a division by zero, which no number equals. The slope of such a line is undefined, meaning the line has no slope at all. Two points of a horizontal line have the same \(y\) instead, so the top of the fraction is \(0\) and the bottom is not, and the quotient is the ordinary number \(0\). The zero is on top for a horizontal line and underneath for a vertical one, and only the second case has no answer.

A slope is one change divided by another, which is what a constant rate was in chapter 6. When \(x\) is a time and \(y\) is a measured amount, the slope is how much \(y\) changes per one unit of \(x\), and its units are the units of \(y\) over the units of \(x\). The next two problems ask for a rate from two readings, then the steeper of two lines.

A tank fills at a steady rate. At \(6\) minutes it holds \(23\) liters and at \(20\) minutes it holds \(58\) liters. Liters plotted against minutes give a straight line. Enter the slope of that line, in liters per minute.
hints: The change in \(y\) is a number of liters and the change in \(x\) is a number of minutes.
The tank gains \(58-23\) liters over \(20-6\) minutes. Reduce the quotient.
blocks.sol: The change is \(58-23=35\) liters over \(20-6=14\) minutes, so \(m=\frac{35}{14}=\boxed{\frac{5}{2}}\). The units of a slope are the units of \(y\) over the units of \(x\), so this line's slope is \(2.5\) liters per minute.

blocks.x: Line \(g\) passes through \((1,2)\) and \((5,20)\). Line \(h\) passes through \((-3,11)\) and \((2,-14)\). One of the two lines is steeper than the other. Enter the slope of the steeper line.
hints: Compute both slopes first. Which line is steeper depends on the size of each slope and not on its sign.
Line \(g\) has slope \(\frac{9}{2}\), which is \(4.5\). Compare that with the size of the slope of line \(h\).
blocks.sol: Line \(g\) has slope \(\frac{20-2}{5-1}=\frac{18}{4}=\frac{9}{2}\) and line \(h\) has slope \(\frac{-14-11}{2-(-3)}=\frac{-25}{5}=-5\). Steepness is measured by \(|m|\), and \(|-5|=5\) is greater than \(\left|\frac{9}{2}\right|=4.5\), so the steeper line has slope \(\boxed{-5}\). The steeper line here is the one with the smaller slope, since a negative slope can still be the larger in size.

blocks.x: Three points are collinear exactly when the two slopes are equal. Points \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) are collinear when one straight line contains all three. If they are, the slope from \(A\) to \(B\) and the slope from \(B\) to \(C\) are both the slope of that one line, so the two values are equal. Through \(B\) there is only one line with a given slope, so if the two values are equal then \(A\) and \(C\) lie on that one line too. For \((9,25)\) earlier the two values were not equal. With one coordinate unknown, setting the two slopes equal gives a single equation in that letter.

The last two problems use the definition backwards. In each one the slope is fixed by other information and a missing coordinate is what the question asks for. Writing the slope condition down leaves one equation in one letter, which is chapter 4's work.
The points \((-2,3)\), \((4,k)\) and \((10,23)\) are collinear, so one straight line passes through all three. Only the middle point has an unknown coordinate. Enter \(k\).
hints: Two of the three points are fully known, so the slope of the line comes from those two alone.
That slope is \(\frac{20}{12}=\frac{5}{3}\), and \((4,k)\) is \(6\) to the right of \((-2,3)\).
blocks.sol: The outer points give \(m=\frac{23-3}{10-(-2)}=\frac{20}{12}=\frac{5}{3}\). From \((-2,3)\) to \((4,k)\) the change in \(x\) is \(6\), so the change in \(y\) is \(6\cdot\frac{5}{3}=10\) and \(k=3+10=\boxed{13}\). Checking the other pair, \((4,13)\) to \((10,23)\) gives \(\frac{10}{6}=\frac{5}{3}\), the same slope.

blocks.x: Line \(u\) passes through \((-6,4)\) and \((2,-8)\). Line \(v\) passes through \((3,-7)\) and \((n,5)\). Line \(v\) is exactly as steep as line \(u\), and \(v\) rises from left to right while \(u\) falls. Enter \(n\).
hints: Find \(u\)'s slope first. Equal steepness means the two slopes have the same size, and a line that rises has a positive slope.
Line \(u\) has slope \(-\frac{3}{2}\), so \(v\) has slope \(\frac{3}{2}\), and \(v\)'s change in \(y\) is \(5-(-7)\).
blocks.sol: Line \(u\) has slope \(\frac{-8-4}{2-(-6)}=\frac{-12}{8}=-\frac{3}{2}\), so both slopes have size \(\frac{3}{2}\), and \(v\) rises, so its slope is \(+\frac{3}{2}\). Then \(\frac{5-(-7)}{n-3}=\frac{12}{n-3}=\frac{3}{2}\) gives \(3(n-3)=24\), so \(n-3=8\) and \(n=\boxed{11}\). Reusing \(-\frac{3}{2}\) for \(v\) gives \(n=-5\), a line falling just like \(u\).

blocks.x: Every slope here came from two points of a line already drawn. A slope can also be known first. Exactly one line passes through a given point with a given slope. Lesson 7.4, Finding the Equation of a Line, turns a point and a slope into that line's equation.

review.x: A line passes through \((-1,-2)\) and \((3,18)\). Enter its slope.
hints: Subtract the coordinates of \((-1,-2)\) from the coordinates of \((3,18)\), and keep that same order in the numerator and the denominator.
The change in \(y\) is \(20\) and the change in \(x\) is \(3-(-1)=4\).
review.sol: \(m=\frac{18-(-2)}{3-(-1)}=\frac{20}{4}=\boxed{5}\). Subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so the numerator is \(20\) and not \(16\).

review.x: A line passes through \((-5,13)\) and \((1,-11)\). Enter its slope.
hints: The second point is lower than the first, so the change in \(y\) is negative.
The change in \(y\) is \(-24\) and the change in \(x\) is \(6\).
review.sol: \(m=\frac{-11-13}{1-(-5)}=\frac{-24}{6}=\boxed{-4}\). A negative slope means the line falls from left to right.

review.x: A line passes through \((-5,-4)\) and \((7,4)\). Enter its slope as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The change in \(y\) is \(4-(-4)\) and the change in \(x\) is \(7-(-5)\).
The quotient is \(\frac{8}{12}\), and \(4\) divides both parts.
review.sol: \(m=\frac{4-(-4)}{7-(-5)}=\frac{8}{12}=\boxed{\frac{2}{3}}\). A slope is reported in lowest terms, so \(\frac{8}{12}\) is not the final form.

review.x: A line passes through \((-2,5)\) and \((6,-11)\). A student computes \(\frac{5-(-11)}{6-(-2)}\) and reports \(2\). Enter the correct slope.
hints: On the top the student subtracted the second point's \(y\) from the first point's, and on the bottom the first point's \(x\) from the second point's.
In the bottom the second point's \(x\) comes first, so on the top the second point's \(y\) has to come first too.
review.sol: Putting the second point first in both, \(m=\frac{-11-5}{6-(-2)}=\frac{-16}{8}=\boxed{-2}\). Subtracting in opposite orders on the top and the bottom flips the sign, so the student's \(2\) has the right size and the wrong sign.

review.x: \(U\) and \(V\) are two points on a line, and \(U\) is to the right of \(V\) and higher than \(V\). Enter the word positive or negative for the sign of the slope of that line.
hints: Slope is the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\), and either point may be first as long as the same one is first in both differences. Take \(V\) as the first point.
Going from \(V\) to \(U\) you move to the right and you move up, so decide whether each of the two changes is greater than zero or less than zero, then divide.
review.sol: Taking \(V\) first, both changes are positive, since \(U\) is to the right of \(V\) and above it, so the slope is \(\boxed{\text{positive}}\). With \(U\) first both changes are negative and the quotient is the same positive number.

review.x: Four lines are given by two points each, \((5,-2)\) and \((5,6)\), then \((-7,3)\) and \((9,3)\), then \((2,-1)\) and \((6,5)\), then \((-8,1)\) and \((-8,-6)\). Enter how many of the four have slope \(0\).
hints: A slope of \(0\) means the change in \(y\) is \(0\) while the change in \(x\) is not \(0\).
Two of the four pairs share their first coordinate, and a line through such a pair is vertical.
review.sol: Only \((-7,3)\) and \((9,3)\) share a \(y\)-coordinate, giving \(\frac{0}{16}=0\), so the count is \(\boxed{1}\). The first and fourth pairs share an \(x\)-coordinate, so those lines are vertical and have no slope rather than slope \(0\), and the third pair gives \(\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}\).

review.x: The line through \((-6,w)\) and \((11,-8)\) has slope \(0\). Enter \(w\).
hints: Write the slope of the line through \((-6,w)\) and \((11,-8)\) as the difference of the \(y\)-coordinates over the difference of the \(x\)-coordinates.
A fraction equals \(0\) only when its numerator is \(0\), so set the numerator equal to \(0\) and solve for \(w\).
review.sol: The slope is \(\frac{-8-w}{11-(-6)}=\frac{-8-w}{17}\), and a fraction equals \(0\) only when its numerator is \(0\), so \(-8-w=0\) and \(w=\boxed{-8}\). The line is horizontal, and every point on a horizontal line has the same \(y\)-coordinate.

review.x: The line through \((c,4)\) and \((-7,19)\) has no slope. Enter \(c\).
hints: Slope is the change in \(y\) over the change in \(x\), and it is undefined exactly when the bottom of that fraction is \(0\).
No slope is not the same as slope \(0\). Slope \(0\) would need the two \(y\)-coordinates to match, and \(4\) and \(19\) are different.
review.sol: The slope is undefined only when the two \(x\)-coordinates are equal, so \(c=\boxed{-7}\). Both points then lie on the vertical line \(x=-7\). The change in \(x\) is \(0\), and division by \(0\) is undefined.

review.x: A candle burns down at a steady rate. After \(9\) minutes it is \(23\) cm tall and after \(24\) minutes it is \(17\) cm tall. Height plotted against time gives a straight line. Enter its slope, in centimeters per minute, as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The change in height is negative, since the candle is shorter later.
Write the two readings as the points \((9,23)\) and \((24,17)\), then divide the change in height by the change in time.
review.sol: \(m=\frac{17-23}{24-9}=\frac{-6}{15}=\boxed{-\frac{2}{5}}\). The candle gets \(0.4\) cm shorter each minute, and the slope is negative because the height decreases as time passes.

review.x: A shipping firm charges by weight. An \(8\) kg parcel costs \(37\) dollars and a \(20\) kg parcel costs \(64\) dollars. Cost plotted against weight gives a straight line. Enter the slope of that line, in dollars per kilogram, as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Dollars per kilogram is a number of dollars divided by a number of kilograms, and both of those are changes from the smaller parcel to the larger one.
Subtract the two costs and subtract the two weights, keeping the same parcel first in both subtractions, then write the quotient in lowest terms.
review.sol: \(m=\frac{64-37}{20-8}=\frac{27}{12}=\boxed{\frac{9}{4}}\). Each extra kilogram adds \(2.25\) dollars.

review.x: Four lines have slopes \(-\frac{5}{2}\), \(\frac{12}{5}\), \(-\frac{7}{4}\) and \(\frac{8}{3}\). Enter the slope of the least steep one.
hints: Steepness is measured by the size of the slope, so compare the four without their signs.
Only one of the four sizes is less than \(2\).
review.sol: The sizes are \(\frac{5}{2}=2.5\), \(\frac{12}{5}=2.4\), \(\frac{7}{4}=1.75\) and \(\frac{8}{3}\approx 2.67\), and the smallest is \(\frac{7}{4}\), so the least steep line has slope \(\boxed{-\frac{7}{4}}\). The minus sign stays, since the question asks for the slope and not for its size.

review.x: Line \(g\) passes through \((0,0)\) and \((7,-24)\). Line \(h\) passes through \((1,-4)\) and \((6,13)\). Enter the slope of the steeper line.
hints: Compute both slopes. Steepness is measured by the absolute value of the slope, so compare the two sizes over a common denominator.
The two sizes are \(\frac{24}{7}\) and \(\frac{17}{5}\). Over \(35\) those are \(\frac{120}{35}\) and \(\frac{119}{35}\).
review.sol: Line \(g\) has slope \(\frac{-24-0}{7-0}=-\frac{24}{7}\) and line \(h\) has slope \(\frac{13-(-4)}{6-1}=\frac{17}{5}\). Steepness is measured by \(|m|\), and \(\frac{24}{7}=\frac{120}{35}\) is greater than \(\frac{17}{5}=\frac{119}{35}\), so the steeper line is \(g\), with slope \(\boxed{-\frac{24}{7}}\). Both sizes round to \(3.4\) at one decimal place, so a rounded check is not enough here.

review.x: A line has slope \(7\) and passes through \((2,-5)\). Another of its points has \(x\)-coordinate \(8\). Enter that point's \(y\)-coordinate.
hints: The slope from \((2,-5)\) to the new point is \(7\), and its change in \(x\) is \(8-2\).
A change of \(6\) in \(x\) with slope \(7\) means a change of \(42\) in \(y\).

review.x: A line passes through \((4,-11)\) and \((4,6)\). Enter its slope, or the word undefined if it has none.
hints: Take the two differences the usual way and look at the bottom of the fraction before dividing.
Both points have \(x\)-coordinate \(4\), so the change in \(x\) is \(0\), and division by \(0\) is not defined.
review.sol: Both points have \(x\)-coordinate \(4\), so the change in \(x\) is \(4-4=0\) and the slope would be \(\frac{6-(-11)}{0}\), a division by zero, so the slope is \(\boxed{\text{undefined}}\). A vertical line has no slope at all, which is not the same as having slope \(0\), and that is the horizontal case.

review.x: The points \((-7,9)\), \((1,-7)\) and \((r,-16)\) lie on one straight line. Enter \(r\).
hints: The first two points are fully known, so they give the slope of the line.
That slope is \(-2\), and from \((1,-7)\) to \((r,-16)\) the change in \(y\) is \(-9\).
review.sol: The first two points give \(m=\frac{-7-9}{1-(-7)}=\frac{-16}{8}=-2\). From \((1,-7)\) to \((r,-16)\) the change in \(y\) is \(-9\), so \(\frac{-9}{r-1}=-2\) gives \(r-1=\frac{9}{2}\) and \(r=\boxed{\frac{11}{2}}\). The unknown here is an \(x\)-coordinate, so it is in the denominator of the slope, which makes the last step a division rather than a multiplication.

review.x: The line through \((-4,3)\) and \((8,12)\) is exactly as steep as the line through \((2,6)\) and \((n,-3)\), and the second line falls from left to right. Enter \(n\).
hints: Find the first line's slope, then decide the sign of the second from the fact that it falls.
The first slope is \(\frac{3}{4}\), so the second is \(-\frac{3}{4}\), and the second line's change in \(y\) is \(-9\).
review.sol: The first line has slope \(\frac{12-3}{8-(-4)}=\frac{9}{12}=\frac{3}{4}\), so the second slope has size \(\frac{3}{4}\), and since that line falls the second slope is \(-\frac{3}{4}\). Then \(\frac{-3-6}{n-2}=\frac{-9}{n-2}=-\frac{3}{4}\) gives \(3(n-2)=36\), so \(n=\boxed{14}\). Taking the second slope as \(+\frac{3}{4}\) instead gives \(n=-10\), and that line rises from left to right.

review.x: The points \((-9,2)\), \((-9,7)\) and \((c,15)\) lie on one straight line. Enter \(c\).
hints: The collinearity check compares two slopes, so find the change in \(x\) from \((-9,2)\) to \((-9,7)\) first and see whether the slope formula gives a number at all.
That change is \(0\), so the slope through the first two points is undefined and the line through them is vertical. Every point on a vertical line shares one \(x\)-coordinate.
review.sol: The first two points both have \(x\)-coordinate \(-9\), so the line through them is the vertical line \(x=-9\), and every point of that line has first coordinate \(-9\), giving \(c=\boxed{-9}\). The change in \(x\) from \((-9,2)\) to \((-9,7)\) is \(0\), so that slope is undefined and the equal-slopes check does not apply.

7.4.title: Finding the Equation of a Line

blocks.x: A slope is a number computed from a line that is already drawn. It can also be known before any line is drawn. One point and a slope, or two points, are enough to write an equation whose graph is that line, and once that equation is written, arithmetic gives every other point of the line.
A line has slope \(3\) and passes through \((2,5)\). The point \((8,y)\) is on that same line, and the slope between any two points of a line is the same. Enter the value of \(y\).
hints: The slope between \((2,5)\) and \((8,y)\) is \(\frac{y-5}{8-2}\), and that has to come out to \(3\).
The denominator is \(6\), so the equation is \(\frac{y-5}{6}=3\). Multiply both sides by \(6\).
blocks.sol: The slope between the two points is \(\frac{y-5}{8-2}=\frac{y-5}{6}\), and that equals \(3\), so \(y-5=18\) and \(y=\boxed{23}\). The slope formula from 7.3 is used the other way round here, with the slope known and one coordinate unknown.

blocks.x: A line has slope \(4\) and passes through \((5,3)\), and \((x,y)\) is any other point on it. The slope between those two points is \(4\), so \(\frac{y-3}{x-5}=4\). Multiply both sides by \(x-5\), expand, and solve for \(y\). The result reads \(y=4x+c\) for one number \(c\). Enter \(c\).
hints: Multiplying both sides by \(x-5\) leaves \(y-3=4(x-5)\), and the \(4\) multiplies both terms inside the parentheses.
Expanding gives \(y-3=4x-20\). Now add \(3\) to both sides.
blocks.sol: Multiplying by \(x-5\) gives \(y-3=4(x-5)=4x-20\), and adding \(3\) to both sides gives \(y=4x-17\), so \(c=\boxed{-17}\). Check at the given point, \(4(5)-17=3\). The constant is not the \(3\) from the point, because the \(-20\) from expanding is added to it.

blocks.x: Point-slope form. Let \((x_1,y_1)\) be a known point of a line with slope \(m\), and let \((x,y)\) be any other point of that line. The slope between the two is \(m\), so \(\frac{y-y_1}{x-x_1}=m\). Multiplying both sides by \(x-x_1\) gives $$y-y_1=m(x-x_1),$$ which is point-slope form. It is built from one point and one slope and nothing else. The multiplied equation is true at \((x_1,y_1)\) as well, where both sides are \(0\), even though the fraction it was cleared from is undefined there, so its solution points are the whole line.
A line has slope \(-4\) and passes through \((-3,8)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(5\).
hints: Write point-slope with \((x_1,y_1)=(-3,8)\). Because \(x_1\) is negative, the factor \(x-x_1\) is \(x+3\) and not \(x-3\).
The line is \(y-8=-4(x+3)\). At \(x=5\) the bracket is \(8\), so multiply that by \(-4\) and then solve for \(y\).
blocks.sol: Point-slope with \((x_1,y_1)=(-3,8)\) and \(m=-4\) gives \(y-8=-4(x+3)\), and at \(x=5\) the right side is \(-4(8)=-32\), so \(y=8-32=\boxed{-24}\). With \(x_1=-3\) the factor \(x-x_1\) is \(x+3\), and using \(x-3\) instead gives \(-4(2)=-8\) and the wrong value \(0\).

blocks.x: A line has slope \(\frac{2}{7}\) and passes through \((3,5)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(8\). It is not a whole number, so enter it as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The run from \(x=3\) to \(x=8\) is \(5\), and the rise is the slope times the run.
The rise is \(\frac{2}{7}(5)=\frac{10}{7}\). Write \(5\) as \(\frac{35}{7}\) before adding.
blocks.sol: The run is \(8-3=5\) and the rise is \(\frac{2}{7}(5)=\frac{10}{7}\), so \(y=5+\frac{10}{7}=\frac{35}{7}+\frac{10}{7}=\boxed{\frac{45}{7}}\). A fractional slope is not a special case. It only means most runs give a \(y\) that is not a whole number.

blocks.x: Substituting the point and the slope. Putting \(m\), \(x_1\) and \(y_1\) into \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\) leaves \(x\) and \(y\) as the only letters, and that is already an equation of the line. Expanding is a separate step. The right side is \(m\) times a difference, so expanding it gives \(y-y_1=mx-mx_1\), and adding \(y_1\) to both sides gives \(y=mx-mx_1+y_1\), the line solved for \(y\). The number added to \(mx\) is \(y_1-mx_1\) and not \(y_1\). Both equations have the same solution points, so both are equations of the same line.

blocks.cap: Many lines pass through the one marked point, so a point alone does not pin a line down. Fixing the slope as well leaves exactly one, drawn bold here with its slope triangle. Those two pieces, a point and a slope, are what point-slope form is built from.

blocks.x: Point-slope form is built from a point and a slope, and two points of a line give both. Either of the two is the point, and \(m\) is the slope computed from the pair. So two points are enough to write the equation of the line through them, and the next two problems do exactly that.
A line passes through \((1,10)\) and \((6,-5)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(8\).
hints: The slope is not stated here. Compute it from \((1,10)\) and \((6,-5)\) first, then use point-slope form with either of those points.
The slope is \(\frac{-5-10}{6-1}=-3\). Now work from \((6,-5)\) with a run of \(2\).
blocks.sol: The slope is \(\frac{-5-10}{6-1}=\frac{-15}{5}=-3\). From \((6,-5)\), the run out to \(x=8\) is \(2\) and the rise is \(-3(2)=-6\), so \(y=-5-6=\boxed{-11}\). Reversing only one of the two differences gives \(+3\) for the slope, and the answer then comes out \(1\) instead.

blocks.x: A line passes through \((-4,3)\) and \((8,11)\). Exactly one point of that line has \(y\)-coordinate \(15\). Enter that point's \(x\)-coordinate.
hints: The number given here is a \(y\)-coordinate, so the unknown is \(x\). Start with the slope of the two given points.
blocks.sol: The slope is \(\frac{11-3}{8-(-4)}=\frac{8}{12}=\frac{2}{3}\). Using \((8,11)\), \(15-11=\frac{2}{3}(x-8)\), so \(4=\frac{2}{3}(x-8)\), then \(x-8=6\) and \(x=\boxed{14}\). Checking with \((-4,3)\), \(\frac{15-3}{14-(-4)}=\frac{12}{18}=\frac{2}{3}\), the same slope. A slope of \(\frac{2}{3}\) does not force a fractional answer, since the run \(\frac{3}{2}\cdot 4\) is whole.

blocks.x: From two points, compute the slope first. Given two points \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\) with different \(x\)-coordinates, compute \(m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\), then substitute that \(m\) and either of the two points into \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\). The order is forced, since point-slope form contains \(m\) and no substitution is possible until \(m\) is a number. Subtract in the same order top and bottom, taking the same point first in both. Mixing the two orders leaves \(m\) with the wrong sign, and unless \(m=0\) the result is an equation of a different line.

There are two choices for \((x_1,y_1)\), one for each of the two points, and every problem so far used only one of them. Choosing the other point puts different numbers into point-slope form, so the two equations do not look alike until one of them is expanded. The next problem rebuilds an earlier line from its other point.

The line through \((1,10)\) and \((6,-5)\) has slope \(-3\). Substitute the point \((6,-5)\) and that slope into point-slope form, expand, and solve for \(y\). The result reads \(y=-3x+c\). Enter \(c\).
hints: With \((x_1,y_1)=(6,-5)\), the left side is \(y-(-5)\), which is \(y+5\).
The equation is \(y+5=-3(x-6)\). Expand the right side before moving the \(5\).
blocks.sol: Substituting gives \(y-(-5)=-3(x-6)\), which is \(y+5=-3x+18\), so \(y=-3x+13\) and \(c=\boxed{13}\). Starting from \((1,10)\) instead gives \(y-10=-3(x-1)\), and that expands to \(y=-3x+13\) as well. The two point-slope equations look different and describe the same line.

blocks.x: In the 1760s Johann Heinrich Lambert drew a straight line through measurements that did not all lie on one, then read values off that line at points he had never measured and used those readings as data.
A line passes through \((-6,-2)\) and \((4,3)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(15\), as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Take \((-6,-2)\) first in both differences of the slope. Both involve subtracting a negative number, so write them out before simplifying.
The slope is \(\frac{3-(-2)}{4-(-6)}=\frac{1}{2}\), so point-slope from \((4,3)\) gives \(y-3=\frac{1}{2}(x-4)\). Put \(x=15\) into that.
blocks.sol: The slope is \(\frac{3-(-2)}{4-(-6)}=\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2}\), so point-slope from \((4,3)\) gives \(y-3=\frac{1}{2}(x-4)\). At \(x=15\) that reads \(y-3=\frac{1}{2}(11)=\frac{11}{2}\), so \(y=\boxed{\frac{17}{2}}\). The \(x\) asked for sits to the right of both given points, and the work is no different from finding \(y\) at an \(x\) between them.

blocks.x: Either point gives the same line. From \((1,10)\) the equation is \(y-10=-3(x-1)\), from \((6,-5)\) it is \(y+5=-3(x-6)\), and expanding either one gives \(y=-3x+13\). That holds in general. Subtracting \(y-y_2=m(x-x_2)\) from \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\) leaves \(y_2-y_1=m(x_2-x_1)\), which is the slope formula with the denominator cleared. It contains no \(x\) and no \(y\), so it is true at every point, and the two equations have the same solution points. Either point is a valid choice, so take the one with the easier arithmetic.

Every pair of points so far had two different \(x\)-coordinates. When the two \(x\)-coordinates are equal, \(x_2-x_1\) is \(0\), the quotient is a division by zero, and the line has no slope at all. Point-slope form contains \(m\), so with no slope there is nothing to substitute into it. The next problem is that case.
A line passes through \((-5,11)\) and \((-5,-6)\). One point on that line has \(y\)-coordinate \(60\). Enter that point's \(x\)-coordinate.
hints: Start with the slope through the two given points, and look hard at the denominator \(x_2-x_1\) before dividing.
There is no slope, so point-slope form cannot be used here at all. Compare the two first coordinates, then recall the vertical lines from 7.2.
blocks.sol: Both given points have first coordinate \(-5\), so this is the vertical line \(x=-5\), and the point with \(y\)-coordinate \(60\) is \((-5,60)\), whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(\boxed{-5}\). The slope \(\frac{-6-11}{-5-(-5)}\) has denominator \(0\), so this line has no slope and point-slope form does not apply. The second coordinate is unrestricted here, so the \(60\) is not needed.

blocks.x: The points \((-4,9)\), \((2,-3)\) and \((k,-13)\) all lie on one straight line. Enter \(k\).
hints: Two of the three points are fully known, and two points are enough to pin the line. Start there.
Find the slope from the two known points, then put that slope and \((2,-3)\) into point-slope form and substitute \(x=k\) and \(y=-13\).
blocks.sol: The first two points give slope \(\frac{-3-9}{2-(-4)}=\frac{-12}{6}=-2\), and from \((2,-3)\), \(-13-(-3)=-2(k-2)\), so \(-10=-2(k-2)\), then \(k-2=5\) and \(k=\boxed{7}\). The line is \(y=-2x+1\), and \(-2(7)+1=-13\) checks it. Three points lie on one line exactly when the third satisfies the equation of the line through the other two.

blocks.x: Two points with the same \(x\)-coordinate give \(x=k\). If \((k,y_1)\) and \((k,y_2)\) are two different points of a line, the slope formula has \(0\) underneath, so the line has no slope and point-slope form does not apply. Every point of that line has first coordinate \(k\), with no condition on the second, so its equation is \(x=k\), the vertical line of 7.2. Two points with the same \(y\)-coordinate are the opposite case. There the slope is \(0\), which is an ordinary number, so point-slope form does apply and gives \(y-y_1=0\), which is \(y=y_1\).

A quantity that changes at a constant rate has a straight line for its graph, and the rate is the slope of that line. Two readings of the quantity are two points of that line, so two readings are enough to determine the whole relationship, including its value at a moment nobody measured.

A machine winds cable onto a drum at a constant rate. Three minutes after the machine starts, the drum holds \(52\) metres of cable, and ten minutes after it starts, the drum holds \(115\) metres. The drum was not empty when the machine started. Enter how many metres of cable the drum held at the moment the machine started.
hints: Time and length are the two coordinates. The readings are the points \((3,52)\) and \((10,115)\), and the constant rate is the slope.
The rate is \(\frac{115-52}{10-3}=9\) metres per minute, so step back \(3\) minutes from the first reading.
blocks.sol: The readings are the points \((3,52)\) and \((10,115)\), so the rate is \(\frac{115-52}{10-3}=\frac{63}{7}=9\) metres per minute. Stepping back \(3\) minutes from \((3,52)\) gives \(52-9(3)=\boxed{25}\). Dividing \(115\) by \(10\) gives \(11.5\), which is the rate only for a drum that starts empty.

blocks.x: A line passes through \((-2,11)\) and \((6,-5)\). Exactly one point of that line has its \(y\)-coordinate equal to three times its \(x\)-coordinate. Enter that point's \(x\)-coordinate, as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Find the equation of the line first. The stated condition describes one point of it and says nothing extra about the line.
The line is \(y=-2x+7\). A point on it whose \(y\)-coordinate is three times its \(x\)-coordinate satisfies \(3x=-2x+7\).
blocks.sol: The slope is \(\frac{-5-11}{6-(-2)}=\frac{-16}{8}=-2\), and from \((-2,11)\), \(y-11=-2(x+2)\), so \(y=-2x+7\). The condition is \(y=3x\), so \(3x=-2x+7\), then \(5x=7\) and \(x=\boxed{\frac{7}{5}}\). The point is \(\left(\frac{7}{5},\frac{21}{5}\right)\), and \(-2\left(\frac{7}{5}\right)+7=\frac{21}{5}\) confirms it.

blocks.x: Nearly every line here came from a point and a slope, and each of those equations was left in point-slope form or solved for \(y\). The exception was the vertical line, which has no slope, so it is written \(x=k\) instead. Lesson 7.5, Intercepts and Standard Forms, gives the two standard ways of writing a line and reads the slope straight off each one.

review.x: A line has slope \(5\) and passes through \((1,2)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(3\).
hints: One point and one slope are given, so use \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\) with \((x_1,y_1)=(1,2)\).
The run is \(3-1=2\), so the rise is \(5(2)\).
review.sol: The run is \(3-1=2\) and the rise is \(5(2)=10\), so \(y=2+10=\boxed{12}\).

review.x: A line has slope \(3\) and passes through \((-1,4)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(5\).
hints: Point-slope form is \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\), and here \(m=3\) with \((x_1,y_1)=(-1,4)\).
review.sol: Point-slope gives \(y-4=3(x-(-1))\), and at \(x=5\) the right side is \(3(6)=18\), so \(y=\boxed{22}\). Checking, the slope from \((-1,4)\) to \((5,22)\) is \(\frac{18}{6}=3\).

review.x: A line has slope \(-4\) and passes through \((6,2)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(9\).
hints: The slope and one point are enough to write the line's equation, using the point-slope form \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\).
The equation is \(y-2=-4(x-6)\). Put \(9\) in for \(x\) and solve for \(y\).
review.sol: Point-slope with \(m=-4\) and \((6,2)\) gives \(y-2=-4(x-6)\). At \(x=9\) that reads \(y-2=-4(3)=-12\), so \(y=\boxed{-10}\). The slope is negative, so the point three to the right of \((6,2)\) lies below it rather than above.

review.x: A line has slope \(5\) and passes through \((4,-3)\). Solved for \(y\), its equation reads \(y=5x+c\). Enter \(c\).
hints: Substitute the slope and the point into point-slope form, \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\), and take care with the sign when \(y_1=-3\).
Expanding gives \(y+3=5x-20\), which is not yet solved for \(y\), so subtract \(3\) from both sides.
review.sol: Point-slope form gives \(y+3=5(x-4)=5x-20\), so \(y=5x-23\) and \(c=\boxed{-23}\). Reading \(c\) off \(y+3=5x-20\) gives \(-20\), which skips the last subtraction. Checking, \(5(4)-23=-3\).

review.x: A line has slope \(\frac{3}{5}\) and passes through \((5,1)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(9\), as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The run is \(9-5=4\), and the rise is the slope times the run.
review.sol: The run is \(4\) and the rise is \(\frac{3}{5}(4)=\frac{12}{5}\), so \(y=1+\frac{12}{5}=\frac{5}{5}+\frac{12}{5}=\boxed{\frac{17}{5}}\).

review.x: A line has slope \(4\) and passes through \((3,-1)\). Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(19\).
hints: Here the \(y\)-coordinate is the one given, so the unknown is \(x\).
Point-slope form gives \(19-(-1)=4(x-3)\), which is \(20=4(x-3)\).

review.x: A line passes through \((2,1)\) and \((5,10)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(8\).
hints: Find the slope from \((2,1)\) and \((5,10)\) first, then write the line through \((5,10)\) with that slope.
The slope is \(\frac{10-1}{5-2}=3\), so the line is \(y-10=3(x-5)\), and \(x=8\) is the value to substitute.
review.sol: The slope is \(\frac{10-1}{5-2}=3\), so the line through \((5,10)\) is \(y-10=3(x-5)\). At \(x=8\), \(y-10=3\cdot 3=9\), so \(y=\boxed{19}\). Using \((2,1)\) instead gives \(y-1=3(x-2)\) and the same \(19\) at \(x=8\).

review.x: A line passes through \((-3,8)\) and \((1,0)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(4\).
hints: Two points fix the slope, the change in \(y\) divided by the change in \(x\). Take \((-3,8)\) first in both subtractions, and subtract the \(0\) in \((1,0)\) like any other coordinate.
The slope is \(\frac{0-8}{1-(-3)}=-2\), and from \((1,0)\) the run out to \(x=4\) is \(3\).
review.sol: The slope is \(\frac{0-8}{1-(-3)}=\frac{-8}{4}=-2\). From \((1,0)\) the run out to \(x=4\) is \(3\), so the rise is \(3\cdot(-2)=-6\) and \(y=0-6=\boxed{-6}\). Measuring the run from \(x=0\) instead of from \(x=1\) gives a run of \(4\) and the wrong value \(-8\).

review.x: A line passes through \((-1,-2)\) and \((3,10)\). Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(28\).
hints: The number given is a \(y\)-coordinate, so solve for \(x\) once the slope is known.

review.x: A line passes through \((-4,3)\) and \((-4,11)\). Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(-60\).
hints: Compare the two \(x\)-coordinates before reaching for the slope formula.
They are equal, so \(x_2-x_1\) is \(0\) and the line has no slope.
review.sol: Both given points have first coordinate \(-4\), so the change in \(x\) is \(0\) and there is no slope. The line is \(x=-4\), so every point on it has \(x=\boxed{-4}\). There is no slope to substitute into point-slope form, so it does not apply here, and the \(-60\) is not needed.

review.x: A line passes through \((-7,5)\) and \((4,5)\). Solved for \(y\), its equation reads \(y=ax+b\) for two numbers \(a\) and \(b\). Enter \(a\).
hints: The coefficient of \(x\) once a line is solved for \(y\) is its slope, so find the slope first.
Both points have \(y\)-coordinate \(5\), so the change in \(y\) is \(0\) while the change in \(x\) is not.
review.sol: The change in \(y\) is \(5-5=0\) and the change in \(x\) is \(4-(-7)=11\), so the slope is \(\frac{0}{11}=0\) and the coefficient of \(x\) is \(\boxed{0}\). The line is horizontal, and every point on it has \(y=5\) whatever \(x\) is.

review.x: The line through \((1,5)\) and \((4,17)\) also passes through \((9,k)\). Enter \(k\).
hints: Two points fix the line, so work out the slope from \((1,5)\) and \((4,17)\) before touching \(k\).
The slope is \(\frac{17-5}{4-1}=4\), so point-slope from \((1,5)\) gives \(y-5=4(x-1)\). Put \(x=9\) into that.
review.sol: The slope is \(\frac{17-5}{4-1}=4\), so point-slope from \((1,5)\) gives \(y-5=4(x-1)\). At \(x=9\), \(k=5+4(8)=\boxed{37}\).

review.x: A line passes through \((-3,2)\) and \((7,10)\). Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of the point on that line whose \(x\)-coordinate is \(4\), as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Neither given point has \(x\)-coordinate \(4\), so find the slope from the two points first and build the line from there.
The slope is \(\frac{10-2}{7-(-3)}=\frac{4}{5}\), and from \((-3,2)\) the run out to \(x=4\) is \(7\).
review.sol: The slope is \(\frac{10-2}{7-(-3)}=\frac{8}{10}=\frac{4}{5}\), so the line is \(y-2=\frac{4}{5}(x+3)\). At \(x=4\) that reads \(y-2=\frac{4}{5}(7)=\frac{28}{5}\), so \(y=\boxed{\frac{38}{5}}\).

review.x: A line passes through \((-6,14)\) and \((2,-2)\). Solve for \(y\) to write its equation as \(y=mx+c\) for two numbers \(m\) and \(c\). Enter \(c\).
hints: The change in \(y\) is \(-2-14\) and the change in \(x\) is \(2-(-6)\), so get the slope first.
Using \((2,-2)\), point-slope form gives \(y+2=-2(x-2)\).

review.x: A candle burns down at a constant rate. It stands \(21\) cm tall \(12\) minutes after it is lit and \(16\) cm tall \(32\) minutes after it is lit. Enter its height in centimeters at the moment it was lit.
hints: The readings are the points \((12,21)\) and \((32,16)\), with time as the first coordinate.
The rate is \(\frac{16-21}{32-12}=-\frac{1}{4}\) cm per minute, so step back \(12\) minutes from the first reading.
review.sol: The rate is \(\frac{16-21}{32-12}=\frac{-5}{20}=-\frac{1}{4}\) cm per minute. Over the \(12\) minutes before the first reading the candle lost \(3\) cm, so its height at the moment it was lit is \(\boxed{24}\). Checking, \(24-\frac{1}{4}\cdot 32=16\), which matches the second reading.

review.x: A tank drains at a constant rate, and time is measured in minutes from the moment it starts draining. At \(3\) minutes it holds \(92\) liters and at \(11\) minutes it holds \(68\) liters. Enter the number of minutes at which it holds \(50\) liters.
hints: The readings are the points \((3,92)\) and \((11,68)\). The question asks for a time, so the unknown is the first coordinate.
The rate is \(-3\) liters per minute, so \(50-92=-3(t-3)\).

review.x: A line passes through \((-6,13)\) and \((-6,-2)\), and the point \((4k,40)\) is on that same line. Enter \(k\).
hints: The two given points share an \(x\)-coordinate, so write down the equation of that line before anything else.
The line is \(x=-6\), and the third point's first coordinate is \(4k\).
review.sol: Both given points have first coordinate \(-6\), so the line has no slope and its equation is \(x=-6\). A point is on it exactly when its first coordinate is \(-6\), so \(4k=-6\) and \(k=\boxed{-\frac{3}{2}}\). The \(40\) is not needed, since \(x=-6\) is true for every value of \(y\).
